title: AI Chip Startup Etched Doubles Valuation to $21 Billion in Under a Month
excerpt: Jane Street-backed semiconductor startup raises $700 million as investors pile into AI inference hardware, challenging Nvidia's dominance.
body:
• Etched raised $700 million in a new funding round led by Jane Street, valuing the company at $21 billion — more than double its $10.3 billion valuation from just weeks earlier.
  • The San Jose startup has signed over $1 billion in customer contracts and begun shipping its AI inference chips, with Jane Street as its first deployed customer.
  • Founded by three 24-year-old Harvard dropouts, Etched has recruited roughly 15% of its 400-person workforce from Nvidia as it challenges the GPU giant in the inference market.

AI chip startup Etched has more than doubled its valuation to $21 billion in less than a month, fueled by surging investor appetite for specialized hardware that can run artificial intelligence models faster and cheaper.

The San Jose, California-based company announced on Tuesday that it raised $700 million in a new round led by Jane Street, the secretive Wall Street quantitative-trading firm that is also Etched's first customer. Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Tiger Global, Bain Capital Ventures, and Blackstone also participated, according to Reuters and The Wall Street Journal.

The round comes just weeks after Etched closed a $300 million Series C at a $10.3 billion valuation, also led by Sequoia. The company has now raised $1.9 billion in total.

From Harvard Dorm to Chip Foundry

Etched was co-founded in 2022 by Gavin Uberti, Chris Zhu, and Robert Wachen — all 24-year-old Harvard dropouts who met in Math 55, the university's famously difficult undergraduate course in theoretical mathematics. The founders entered a semiconductor industry where conventional wisdom held that young entrepreneurs had no business building chips.

https://x.com/Jeremybtc/status/2089775519646798168

"There was a sense that these kids think they can do anything, and maybe on the internet, they can, but that in chips, startups are guilty until proven innocent."

— Sonya Huang, General Partner, Sequoia Capital

The startup builds specialized AI inference systems — hardware designed to make trained AI models generate responses faster and more cheaply. It's a market segment growing rapidly as companies shift from training models to deploying them at scale. Etched says it took just 44 days to get its test chips from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing running inference workloads, a process that typically takes six months or more.

"We may be the only AI chip that was built by a startup that was successful on the first try," co-founder Robert Wachen told The Wall Street Journal.

Poaching Nvidia's Best

What sets Etched apart from other chip startups is both the speed of its execution and the depth of its engineering bench. Around 15% of the company's roughly 400 employees previously worked at Nvidia, the dominant force in AI chips. The exodus includes Brian Loiler, a former top systems engineer who spent nearly 23 years at Nvidia, and Saptadeep Pal, a former Nvidia researcher who became Etched's chief silicon architect.

"One leaves, and then another one, you hear a couple weeks later, and you go, 'Whoa, I can't believe so-and-so is heading over to Etched,'" systems engineer Anthony Gamerman, who joined from Nvidia in April, told the Journal.

The company has also targeted quantitative trading firms as both customers and investors. Tim Perevozchikov, a former quant trader at Two Sigma, was recruited to head finance operations. The move makes strategic sense: trading firms demand the fastest processors available, willing to pay a premium for even fractions of a second in computing advantage.

Shipping Product, Not Just Promises

Unlike many AI hardware startups still in the prototype phase, Etched has begun shipping. Jane Street received its first server rack last month and is now deploying Etched chips in production workloads. The startup claims its chip architecture and custom interconnections allow communication tasks to be performed in 700 nanoseconds — compared to approximately 4,000 nanoseconds on Nvidia's Blackwell processors.

Etched has also invested heavily in vertical integration, maintaining a 20-person team in Taiwan where it owns a factory that builds server components. The company handles nearly all chip testing in-house rather than outsourcing it, and operates a 2-megawatt data center at its San Jose offices for customer demos and testing.

The $21 billion valuation puts Etched above the $20 billion that Nvidia paid to acquire Groq's technology and leadership last December, underscoring how fiercely competitive the AI inference chip market has become.

What's Next

Etched says it has secured more than $1 billion in customer contracts across public and private AI companies as well as cloud providers, though it has not named customers beyond Jane Street or disclosed contract terms. The company's claims about chip performance remain self-reported — no third-party benchmark data on token throughput, latency, or power efficiency has been published.

Still, the speed of Etched's ascent — from a $5 billion valuation in late 2025 to $21 billion in August 2026 — reflects the broader frenzy around AI infrastructure. With demand for inference computing expected to grow as AI models become ubiquitous in consumer and enterprise applications, investors are placing big bets that Nvidia's dominance won't go unchallenged.
